text:
Recent work supports learning directional continuation signals separately from item similarity. [DTR4Rec (2024 online/2025 volume)](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10489-024-05875-3) counts long-window directed transitions and short-window co-occurrences, then learns their fusion with sequence predictions; its experiments include Amazon Beauty and Sports. [GLSRec (2026)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0169023X26000534) combines lightweight graph propagation, global transition calibration of item embeddings, and local MLP sequence mixers. [Revisiting Graph Projections (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.09209) offers a simpler complementary-product approach using a directed weighted projection of historical user–item interactions. These motivate inexpensive transition-based additions before a larger GNN.

Complementarity and substitution require care: [TransGAT (ICDM 2024)](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/10884336/) explicitly encodes behavioral direction and jointly models complement/substitute graphs, but observed next-item transitions alone do not establish either relationship. For this benchmark, a proposed adaptation—not a verified result—is a separate sparse directed graph per category, built exclusively from training histories, with distinct source/target embeddings or incoming/outgoing aggregation and a learned residual score alongside SASRec. Optional title/description features could use locally fitted TF-IDF projections or randomly initialized pooled token embeddings trained jointly. Keep this text branch auxiliary; validate graph-only, text-only, and combined additions using macro validation HR@10. No cited result establishes gains on the exact four-category pinned protocol.
